image.depicts:
Lavani (Marathi: लावणी) is a genre of music popular in Maharashtra, India.[1] Lavani is a combination of traditional song and dance, which particularly performed to the beats of Dholki, a percussion instrument. Lavani is noted for its powerful rhythm. Lavani has contributed substantially to the development of Marathi folk theatre.[2] In Maharashtra and southern Madhya Pradesh, it is performed by the female performers wearing nine-yard long sarees. The songs are sung in a quick tempo.

Malian instruments of the Maninka, Wasulu, and Tuareg peoples are now known globally
thanks to their various styles of popular music.

The kora harp-lute and ngoni lute are
central instruments of Maninka jeliw ?
musicians board into a professional lineage.
The ngoni was traditionally played solo
and in mixed-instruments ensembles,
ngoni groups are a recent development.

Increasingly well known are the Maninka
sinbi hunters harp and Wasulu hunters'
instruments. Both Maninka and Wasulu
musicians are regarded as holders of deep
Malian traditions. Today, Wasulu hunters
and musicians are feared and respected
for their command of nyama ?, a spiritual
force encountered during the hunt and

in performances of music. The doriso ?
ngoni harp-lute is one of their most
important instruments.

Northern Mali cultures include the Songhai
and Tuareg, whose lutes and one-stringed
fiddles resemble Maninka and Wasulu
instruments.



I read about this place on Trip Adviser - it was the top rated attraction in Phoenix - and now we can see why! The museum is dedicated to musical instruments from around the world - the collection is fascinating, the exhibits are great and the hands-on displays were fun. We spent almost 5 hours here and still felt rushed - this place is definitely worth a detour.
I know nothing about musical instruments so if you happen to know what a particular instrument is, please feel free to comment on it. I tried to include as many labels as possible.
The museum is in Phoenix, AZ - we visited it in March 2014.

image.title: Khattak Dance
image.creator: amir taj
image.attribution: amir taj, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
image.depicts: Khattak is a swift martial sword-dance of the Khattak tribe of Pashtuns in Pakistan and Afghanistan. It is one of the Pashtun folk dances known as Atanr, not the classical Indian style of dance known as Kathak. Katthak is danced to fast music featuring the piper clarion and drums beaten with sticks. Up to 40 men dance together wielding swords or handkerchiefs, performing acrobatic feats. The fast tempo of Khattak distinguishes it from other Atanr which start slow and pick up speed as the dance progresses. Khattak dancers also lack Sanrry, the distinctive hairstyle.

image.title: The Low Country "Garayak" dance
image.creator: Iamironviper
image.attribution: Iamironviper, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
image.depicts:
This is performance of Sri Lankan traditional dance called the low country "Garayak" dance. Low country garayak dance is a traditional dance form that originated in the southern coastal region of Sri Lanka. It is a highly rhythmic and energetic dance that is performed to the beats of a unique drum called "gara yak bera."
The dance is typically performed by a group of male dancers who wear colorful costumes and masks. The costumes are designed to represent various characters such as demons, animals, and humans. The masks are made of wood and are intricately carved to depict the character being portrayed.

This video was recorded in the final procession of the annual Esala Festival of the historic Ruhunu Kataragama Maha Temple which was held on 11th August 2022 with the participation of a large number of devotees.

image.title: Türkülerin Başına Gelenler Politik-İdeolojik Sebeplerle Değiştirilen Türküler Üzerine
image.creator: Mustafa Dinç
image.attribution: Mustafa Dinç, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
image.depicts:
Abstract
Folk songs are common examples of folk poetry in many areas of social life and are said in almost every subject. As a result of this prevalence, folk songs, which perform many overt or secret functions in line with all the functions of folklore products, have been used to reflect political-ideological ideas from time to time and even some or all of their lyrics have been changed for this purpose. In Turkey, folk songs, which have been restructured by right or left political ideologies, have been used as a propaganda tool in times of intense political activity or in election squares. In the study, which briefly emphasized the political and social conditions of the folk tradition in our country since the second half of the twentieth century, it was determined that it was replaced by political-ideological purposes by the performers who belonged to different ideological trends, especially from the 60s until today. were compared with their performances and repertoire records, and then the ways in which these changes were made were discussed. In this respect, it was determined that these changes were made in the sample folk songs, which were used as arguments of some political movements in various periods by making significant changes to their lyrics for political-ideological reasons, in the form of secularizing, conservationizing, articulating current ideological jargon to the verbal texture of the folk songs and adapting new lyrics to the melodic structure of the The study also required that this situation be considered completely separate from the concepts of variant or version.; it was concluded that it would be more accurate to consider the above practices as a censorship or adaptation.
Keywords

folk song, politics, ideology, censorship, adaptation

image.title: Bekir Sıdkı Sezgin’e Âit Muhayyer Sümbüle Ayin-i Şerifi’nin Biçim Özellikleri Açısından Tahlîli
image.creator: Sitki AKARSU
image.attribution: Sitki AKARSU, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
image.depicts:
Mevlevi literatüründe Ayin-i Şerif olarak geçen formlar, günümüzde Mevlevi Ayini olarak da ifade edilmektedir. Sözlerine “Nutk-ı şerif” denilen Ayin-i şeriflerin güfteleri, Farsça’dır. Sözlerinde de, Allah’ın, peygamberin ve tarikat pirlerinin isimleri zikredilmektedir. Türk musikisi açısından da ayrı ve önemli bir yeri olan bu formlar, müzikal yönü ve anlam bütünlüğü olarak her zaman üst düzey bir besteciliğin ürünü olmuştur. Bölümleri olan “Selam” kısımları bile ayrı manaları içeren belirli temalardaki sözlerden meydana gelmiştir. Yaklaşık 160’ın üzerinde yazılmış olan Ayin-i Şeriflerden biri de, Bekir Sıdkı Sezgin tarafından bestelenmiş olan, Muhayyer Sümbüle Ayin-i Şerif’idir.
Yapılan bu çalışmada, Muhayyer Sümbüle Ayin-i Şerif’i biçim özellikleri yönü ile incelenmiş, belirli bulgulara ulaşılmıştır. Nitel araştırma yöntemlerinden, betimsel tarama modelindeki bu çalışmada, Gülçin Yahya Eser Tahlîli Yöntemi kullanılmıştır. Bu tahlil yöntemi ile Âyine ait usûl, ölçü, cümle, bölüm, makam ve güfte yapılarını gösteren eser kurgusu ile icrâ akışı tabloları verilmiş ayrıca açıklanmıştır. Yapılan çalışmadaki Ayin-i şerifin “Selam” olarak nitelendirilen kısımları da, eserin bölümlerini oluşturmaktadır. Ayin-i şerifler 4 selamdan oluştuğundan, eser de 4 bölümden oluşmaktadır. Bu bölümlerdeki usuller de, ayinlerde tercih edilen usullerden seçilmiştir. I. Selamda Devr-i Revân usulü(14/8), II. Selamda Mevlevî Evferi olarak ta nitelendirilen Ağır Evfer(9/4), III. Selamda Devr-i Kebir(28/4), Aksak Semai(10/8) ve Yürük Semâî(6/8) ile IV. Selamda da yine Ağır Evfer usûlleri kullanılmıştır. Bu 4 bölümde toplam 32 müzik cümlesi tespit edilmiştir. Muhayyer sümbüle Ayin-i şerifi, birbirinden farklı 32 müzik cümlesinden meydana gelmiştir. Bestekar sayın Sezgin, eserinde cümle içlerindeki mısralara bağlı dönüşlerdeki ezgi kalıpları hariç(bu da aynı müzik cümlesi değil, kendi içerisindeki dönüş melodileridir) hep farklı müzik cümleleri tercih etmiştir. Bu tercih, eseri olabildiğine zenginleştirmiş ve müzik cümlelerinde farklı makam geçkileri yaparak Ayin-i şerifi muazzam bir yapıya kavuşturmuştur. Ayin-i şeriflerde Mesnevi-i Şerif’ten, Divân-ı Kebîr’den ve Ahmed Eflâkî Dede’den alınan sözler dışında, lafızlar ve lafzi terennümler kullanılmıştır. Çalışma sonucunda, Muhayyer Sümbüle Ayin-i Şerif’inin toplamda 251 ölçüden oluştuğu belirlenmiştir. Ayrıca eser içerisinde bestekârın birçok makama atıf ve geçki yaptığı tespit edilmiştir.

image.title: Gèlèdé
image.creator: Michaël Wittmer
image.attribution: Michaël Wittmer, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
image.depicts: Le Gèlèdé, Gèlèdè, ou Guèlèdé, est une cérémonie pratiquée par la communauté Yoruba-Nago établie dans la région Yoruba-Nago au Bénin, au Nigeria et au Togo. Des chants en langue yoruba, de la musique par quatre tambours et des danses masquées ont lieu à la fin des récoltes, et lors d'événements importants comme certaines naissances, certains décès, et mariages ou en cas de sécheresse ou d'épidémie. Les effets impressionnants de la cérémonie font dire au peuple yoruba que « les yeux qui ont vu le Gèlèdé ont vu le spectacle ultime » (oju to ba ri Gelede, ti de opin iran). « Le patrimoine oral Gèlèdé » a été originellement proclamé en 2001 puis inscrit en 2008 par l'UNESCO sur la liste représentative du patrimoine culturel immatériel de l'humanité. Photo d’une exposition du château Vodou de Strasbourg.

image.title: Mak Yong Bintan
image.creator: Amriyadibahar
image.attribution: Amriyadibahar, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
image.depicts:
MAK Yong adalah seni tradisi Melayu yang menggabungkan unsur tari dan musik (disertai nyanyian pelakonnya), serta tutur cerita. Kesenian ini dimulai dengan ritus sakral yang disebut upacara ‘buka tanah’ dan diakhiri dengan ritual serupa. Mak Yong konon berasal dari Nara Yala, daerah Patani (saat ini masuk wilayah Thailand Selatan). Dari sana, kesenian itu kemudian menyebar ke Kelantan (Malaysia) sekitar 200 tahun yang lalu. Dari Kelantan, Mak Yong lantas masuk Singapura, kemudian menyeberang ke Riau, Indonesia. Kisah Mak Yong di Indonesia menarik untuk ditelaah dan dipelajari sebagai warisan budaya tak benda yang memperlihatkan keterkaitan budaya Melayu di tiga negara berbeda.
Banyak kisah disampaikan mengenai asal dan makna Mak Yong, dari kisah yang sifatnya sakral, dongeng, hingga ke pemaparan akademis dari para ahli. Jeanne Cuisinier dalam Dances Magiques de Kelantan (1931), misalnya, mengartikan Mak Yong sebagai roh leluhur (Mo Yang ‘nenek’ dan Po Yang ‘datuk’). Menurutnya, Mak Yong berasal dari Main Puteri, yaitu sejenis upacara pengobatan yang dilakukan dengan iringan tarian dan nyanyian. Adapun Walter William Skeat dalam Malay Magic Being: An Introduction to the Folklore and Popular Religion of the Malay Peninsula (1967) berpendapat, Mak Yong berasal dari kata Mak Hiang yang berarti roh ibu atau roh padi.
Mak Yong bersifat sakral karena pada setiap pertunjukannya diawali dan diakhiri dengan ritual ‘buka tanah’ dan ‘tutup tanah’ yang dilakukan oleh seorang bomoh, orang yang khusus memiliki keahlian dalam bidang supranatural. Para pemain, termasuk di dalamnya para pemusik dan penari, diberi air dan mantra yang dipercaya dapat membuat mereka bermain dengan baik. Semua peralatan yang dipakai dalam pementasan juga diberi mantra. Secara khusus, pemeran utama, topeng, dan peralatan musik berupa gendang dan rebab diberi lagi mantra dan jimat lain. Pada upacara buka tanah, bomoh meminta izin dan minta maaf kepada para leluhur. Selama upacara ini berlangsung, tidak boleh ada seorang pun yang melintas di depan arena pertunjukan karena dikhawatirkan mengganggu ‘yang tidak kelihatan’. Setelah upacara ini selesai, lagu Menghadap Rebab dengan tari Ular Sawah dipertunjukkan. Kemudian cerita Mak Yong dimulai dengan lagu pembukaannya, Betabik. image.depicts:
Extract (15 min 03 s) from a field recording of a traditional nighttime Aka ceremony recorded in a forest camp approximately four to five hours' walk south of Bayanga, in the Dzanga-Sangha Special Reserve, Central African Republic, in August 2014.
The recording includes traditional polyphonic singing, percussion and natural rainforest sounds. It was recorded during a ceremony associated with the forest spirits in Aka tradition.
The original recording lasts approximately 2 hours and 40 minutes. This file is an edited excerpt intended to illustrate the characteristic musical structure and atmosphere of the ceremony.

Recorded by Josep M. Gracia.

image.title: Türkülerin Başına Gelenler Politik-İdeolojik Sebeplerle Değiştirilen Türküler Üzerine
image.creator: Mustafa Dinç
image.attribution: Mustafa Dinç, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
image.depicts:
Abstract
Folk songs are common examples of folk poetry in many areas of social life and are said in almost every subject. As a result of this prevalence, folk songs, which perform many overt or secret functions in line with all the functions of folklore products, have been used to reflect political-ideological ideas from time to time and even some or all of their lyrics have been changed for this purpose. In Turkey, folk songs, which have been restructured by right or left political ideologies, have been used as a propaganda tool in times of intense political activity or in election squares. In the study, which briefly emphasized the political and social conditions of the folk tradition in our country since the second half of the twentieth century, it was determined that it was replaced by political-ideological purposes by the performers who belonged to different ideological trends, especially from the 60s until today. were compared with their performances and repertoire records, and then the ways in which these changes were made were discussed. In this respect, it was determined that these changes were made in the sample folk songs, which were used as arguments of some political movements in various periods by making significant changes to their lyrics for political-ideological reasons, in the form of secularizing, conservationizing, articulating current ideological jargon to the verbal texture of the folk songs and adapting new lyrics to the melodic structure of the The study also required that this situation be considered completely separate from the concepts of variant or version.; it was concluded that it would be more accurate to consider the above practices as a censorship or adaptation.
Keywords

folk song, politics, ideology, censorship, adaptation

image.title: 000516 Het Nabije Oosten web (programmaboekje)
image.creator: deSingel
image.attribution: deSingel, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
image.depicts: Een kleine dame met zachte ogen en een magische stem, uit een dorpje dicht bij het legendarische Samarkand. Ze leerde de oude traditionele liederen van haar moeder en zong samen met haar op huwelijksfeesten, rituelen, oogstfeesten. Alle populaire Oezbeekse muziek werd haar van kleins af aan bijgebracht. Op de radio werd ze geconfronteerd met de klassieke muziek van meesters als Barno Eshagova. Matlubeh schreef vlijtig de teksten over en leerde ook dit repertoire. Gesteund door haar moeder die haar kinderen maar wat graag een muziekcarrière zag beginnen, trok ze naar het conservatorium waar ze het geluk had te werken met Aref Khan Hatemov en Turgun Alimatov, twee grootmeesters van de klassieke Oezbeekse muziek. Zij hebben Matlubeh muzikaal gevormd. Al snel werd zij een vaste waarde in haar land. Ze maakt deel uit van het Ensemble Shashmaqam van de nationale radio. De nationale televisie maakte een documentaire over haar carrière. De oorsprong van de muziek in Oezbekistan gaat terug tot de vierde eeuw vóór onze tijdrekening. Niet alleen in teksten maar ook in archeologische opgravingen vinden we bewijzen terug van een rijke muzikale traditie die deel uitmaakte van deze oude beschaving. Matlubeh brengt een programma van het klassieke repertoire, met rijk geschakeerde melodieën volgens de Maqam-traditie, heel dicht bij de oude Perzische muziek.

entries.name: Kabyle popular music
entries.note: Kabyle popular music is a Berber-language genre from the Kabylie region of northern Algeria, blending Amazigh melodic traditions with Western instrumentation; Idir's 1973 recording 'A Vava Inouva' brought the form international recognition, and it remains a vehicle for Tamazight cultural identity alongside contemporary production.

research.period: Idir's international breakthrough 1973 establishes earliest verifiable modern date. Genre continues actively today.
research.geography: Kabylie region (Tizi Ouzou, Béjaïa wilayas) in northern Algeria; Algiers diaspora scene secondary node.
research.artists: Idir (international hit 1973), Lounès Matoub (active 1970s–1998), Takfarinas (1980s–present). All Wikipedia-verified.

entries.name: Amapiano
entries.note: Amapiano is a South African house music sub-genre developed in Pretoria and Johannesburg townships from around 2012, characterised by piano-driven rhythm sections, log-drum bass lines and soulful vocal samples; it reached mainstream and international prominence from 2017 and became one of Africa's most exported contemporary music styles.

research.geography: Emerged in Gauteng (Pretoria/Johannesburg townships); now national and diasporic.
research.artists: Kabza de Small and DJ Maphorisa (duo Scorpion Kings) are the defining artists; Focalistic extended its reach.

entries.name: South African bubblegum
entries.note: South African bubblegum (sa bubblegum) is a synth-pop genre that peaked in the late 1980s, blending disco-era rhythms with Sotho, Zulu and Tsonga lyrics; Brenda Fassie, Chicco Twala and Yvonne Chaka Chaka were its defining voices, and the genre bridged the gap between township mbaqanga and the post-apartheid kwaito era.

research.geography: Johannesburg and Soweto township music industry.
research.artists: Brenda Fassie 'Weekend Special' (1983), Yvonne Chaka Chaka. Both Wikipedia-verified.

entries.name: Sungura
entries.note: Sungura is a Zimbabwean popular dance music genre that developed in Harare from the early 1980s, drawing on Kenyan benga guitar rhythms with driving bass lines and call-and-response vocals in Shona; it remains the most widely consumed grassroots popular genre in Zimbabwe, with Alick Macheso maintaining its commercial dominance.

research.geography: Harare and its townships; most popular in Mashonaland (northern Zimbabwe).
research.artists: Alick Macheso (b. 1969) is the genre's dominant figure. Tongai Moyo (1974–2011).

entries.name: ZimDancehall
entries.note: ZimDancehall is a Zimbabwean genre fusing Jamaican dancehall rhythms with Shona and Ndebele lyrics, developed in Harare's low-income suburbs from around 2000; Soul Jah Love and Winky D established it as the voice of urban Zimbabwean youth and it subsequently gained listeners across southern Africa.

research.geography: Harare; spread nationally.
research.artists: Soul Jah Love (1986–2021) pioneered the genre; Winky D remains its leading voice.

entries.name: Pandza
entries.note: Pandza is a Mozambican urban popular genre developed in Maputo in the 1990s, blending kwaito and marrabenta rhythms with local vernacular Portuguese lyrics; it emerged as the post-civil-war commercial sound of southern Mozambique and remains the dominant contemporary pop style in Maputo's entertainment industry.

research.geography: Maputo metropolitan area; southern Mozambique.

entries.name: Rwandan popular music
entries.note: Contemporary Rwandan popular music (ugushake) emerged in Kigali from around 2000, combining East African dancehall, Congolese rumba and US hip-hop influences with Kinyarwanda and French lyrics; the post-genocide reconstruction era produced a commercially active scene in which artists such as Tom Close and Knowless Butera built regional followings.

research.geography: Kigali; nationally distributed via radio and streaming.

entries.name: Guinean popular music
entries.note: Guinean popular music (Conakry manding pop) emerged from state-sponsored orchestras of the 1960s, grafting Mande griot melodic tradition onto Cuban son and jazz rhythms; Bembeya Jazz Nacional, Guinea's national band, became the archetype, and a continuous lineage of electric Mande pop has persisted in Conakry through contemporary artists.

research.geography: Conakry (south-west Guinea); Mande-speaking zone of western Guinea.
research.artists: Bembeya Jazz Nacional founded 1961; Mory Kanté (1950–2020) achieved international fame.

entries.name: Ethio-pop
entries.note: Ethio-pop is a contemporary Ethiopian popular music genre that emerged in Addis Ababa after the fall of the Derg in 1991, synthesising Amharic lyrical traditions with electronic production, R&B and dancehall influences; Teddy Afro, Aster Aweke and Ejigayehu Shibabaw (Gigi) define its global profile alongside a large domestic music industry.

research.geography: Addis Ababa; nationally distributed.
research.artists: Teddy Afro (b. 1976) is the dominant figure; Aster Aweke active from 1980s.

entries.name: Sinhala popular music
entries.note: Sinhala popular music is a Western-influenced vocal genre in the Sinhala language, developed from the 1960s through Sri Lanka Broadcasting Corporation programmes and Sinhala cinema; Nanda Malini and Sunil Edirisinghe established its lyrical ballad tradition, which continues with contemporary rock and pop productions from Colombo.

research.geography: Colombo and Galle coastal region; SLBC radio gave national reach.
research.artists: Nanda Malini (b. 1945) is the iconic voice; active since 1960s.

entries.name: Bangla pop
entries.note: Bangla pop is a Bangladeshi popular music genre that emerged from Dhaka's rock band scene of the 1980s, developing an acoustic-electric style distinct from Indian film music; bands such as LRB (Love Runs Blind) and James defined its sound through the 1990s, and the genre remains the dominant commercial music of Bangladesh.

research.geography: Dhaka; nationally distributed via television and cassette from 1980s.
research.artists: James (Nagar Baul) remains the most iconic voice; LRB formed 1991.

entries.name: Pakistani pop music
entries.note: Pakistani pop music emerged from Karachi and Lahore from the 1970s, with Nazia Hassan's 1980 'Aap Jaisa Koi' — Pakistan's first international pop crossover — marking its commercial breakthrough; the genre synthesises Urdu lyrical traditions with Western pop production, and Coke Studio's sessions from 2008 renewed international interest in Pakistani popular forms.

research.geography: Karachi and Lahore; two distinct industry hubs.
research.artists: Nazia Hassan (1965–2000) first international hit 1980; Junoon (1990–2004) alt-rock breakthrough.

entries.name: Filmi (Hindi film music)
entries.note: Filmi (Hindi film music) is the popular song genre produced for Bollywood cinema, the world's most prolific film industry; originating in Mumbai from the first Indian sound film in 1931, it blends Hindustani raga structures with Western orchestration and folk elements, with playback singers Lata Mangeshkar and Mohammed Rafi defining its golden age and A.R. Rahman modernising it from the 1990s.

research.geography: Mumbai (Bollywood); distributed nationally and globally via diaspora.
research.artists: Lata Mangeshkar (1929–2022) recorded for 70+ years; A.R. Rahman (b. 1967) from 1992.

entries.name: Khalīji
entries.note: Khalīji is the dominant popular song genre of the Gulf Arab states, practised across the UAE, and characterised by sawt-derived melodies, call-and-response vocal textures, and the leywah and samri rhythmic cycles; it was commercialised from the mid-1970s through cassette distribution and satellite television, and continues as a major pop form alongside Western-influenced Gulf pop.

sources.citation: Lisa Urkevich, 'Khalījī,' in Richard C. Jankowsky, ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

research.period: Bloomsbury dates commercial Khalīji to mid-1970s cassette era. Still active 2026.
research.geography: National scope, UAE. Major scene in Abu Dhabi and Dubai.
research.artists: Hussain Al-Jasmi (b.1981), Majid Al-Muhandis (Iraqi-UAE crossover), Balqees Fathi (b.1988). All Wikipedia-verified.

entries.name: Khalīji
entries.note: Khalīji is the principal popular song tradition of Bahrain, sharing the Gulf-wide leywah and samri rhythmic vocabulary but with a distinctive Bahraini vocal ornamentation; Bahrain's position as an early Gulf media centre helped establish local Khalīji artists on the pan-Arab cassette market from the late 1970s.

sources.citation: Lisa Urkevich, 'Khalījī,' in Richard C. Jankowsky, ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

research.geography: National scope.
research.artists: Khalid Al Sheikh (b.1962), Nabeel Shuail (Kuwaiti but widely Bahraini scene), Shams. Wikipedia-verified.

entries.name: Khalīji
entries.note: Khalīji is Kuwait's principal popular song genre, anchored in the sawt tradition of the pearl-diving era and commercialised from the mid-1970s; Kuwaiti artists helped define the pan-Gulf cassette style through TV variety programmes on Kuwait Television and remain prominent on the contemporary streaming scene.

sources.citation: Lisa Urkevich, 'Khalījī,' in Richard C. Jankowsky, ed., Bloomsbury Encyclopedia of Popular Music of the World, vol. X: Genres: Middle East and North Africa, Bloomsbury Academic, 2015.

entries.name: Khalīji

research.geography: National scope.

entries.name: Syrian popular song
entries.note: Syrian popular song is an Arabic-language urban vocal genre that consolidated in Damascus and Aleppo from the 1970s, combining Egyptian-influenced orchestral arrangements with Syrian maqam ornamentation; artists such as George Wassouf and Asala Nasri achieved pan-Arab popularity, and the scene continues across diaspora communities following the 2011 conflict.

research.period: 1970s commercial scene. Continued by diaspora post-2011.
research.geography: National scope; major centres Damascus and Aleppo.
research.artists: George Wassouf (b.1961, Syrian-Lebanese), Asala Nasri (b.1969, Syrian), Wael Kfoury (b.1971, Lebanese-Syrian crossover).

entries.name: Modern Iraqi song
entries.note: Modern Iraqi song is a Baghdad-centred popular vocal genre distinct from the classical maqam tradition, emerging in the 1950s through radio and cinema; Nazem Al-Ghazali brought international prominence to the form, and Kadim Al Saher later developed it into pan-Arab pop with literary Arabic lyrics, maintaining a substantial audience across the Middle East and diaspora.

research.period: 1950s Baghdad radio era. Nazem Al-Ghazali (1921-1963) key early figure. Ongoing.
research.geography: National scope; Baghdad primary centre.
research.artists: Kadim Al Saher (b.1956), Nazem Al-Ghazali (1921-1963), Ilham Al-Madfai (b.1945). Wikipedia-verified.

entries.name: Georgian popular music
entries.note: Georgian popular music is a post-Soviet urban genre that emerged following independence in 1991, blending Georgian polyphonic vocal tradition with Western pop, rock, and electronic influences; Tbilisi-based artists compete in Eurovision and collaborate with international producers, while the city's electronic music scene has gained global recognition since the 2010s.

research.period: Independence 1991 marks commercial pop launch. Ongoing.
research.geography: National scope; Tbilisi primary centre.
research.artists: Tamara Gverdtsiteli (b.1962), Nino Katamadze (b.1972), Irakli Charkviani (b.1960). Wikipedia-verified.

entries.name: Kyrgyz popular music
entries.note: Kyrgyz popular music is an urban vocal genre that developed following independence in 1991, often combining komuz-derived melodic lines with contemporary electronic production; it coexists with the epic Manas oral tradition and Soviet-era estrada (variety) song, and artists perform in both Kyrgyz and Russian for domestic and Central Asian audiences.

research.period: Post-Soviet independence 1991. Present.
research.geography: National scope; Bishkek primary centre.
research.artists: Mirbek Atabekov (b.1981), Gulzat Mamytbekova, Meerim Usenova. Wikipedia-partial.

entries.name: Turkmen popular music
entries.note: Turkmen popular music is a state-mediated urban song form that developed following independence in 1991, merging Soviet-era estrada style with Turkmen language lyrics and dutar-inflected melodic contours; it operates largely under state broadcast oversight and is distinct from the classical bakhshi epic singing tradition, which continues among specialist practitioners.

research.period: Independence 1991. State-managed. Present.
research.geography: National scope; Ashgabat primary centre.
research.artists: Mähriban Nuryyewa, Aýna Pirliýewa. Wikipedia-limited; state broadcast records.

entries.name: Mongolian popular music
entries.note: Mongolian popular music is an Ulaanbaatar-centred genre that emerged with democratisation in 1990, encompassing rock, pop, and hip-hop alongside traditional khoomei (throat singing) influences; groups like The HU have brought Mongolian rock to global audiences by fusing nomadic instruments with heavy metal, while K-pop-influenced idol pop dominates domestic charts.

research.period: Democracy transition 1990 launches commercial pop. Present.
research.geography: National scope; Ulaanbaatar primary centre.
research.artists: The HU (formed 2016), Nomin Talst (b.1979), Tserenpuntsag Tserendorj. Wikipedia-verified.

entries.name: Cypriot laïkó
entries.note: Cypriot laïkó is the island's dominant popular song genre, sharing the Greek mainland laïkó tradition of orchestral bouzouki-led arrangements but with local Cypriot dialect and performance culture; Cyprus has produced internationally recognised artists who have crossed into the pan-Greek market and Eurovision, and the genre remains the primary commercial pop form in the Greek-Cypriot community.

research.period: 1960s laïkó broadcasting era. Present.
research.geography: National scope; Limassol and Nicosia primary centres.
research.artists: Anna Vissi (b.1958 Cyprus, major Greek-market career), Michalis Hatzigiannis (b.1975), Evridiki (b.1968). Wikipedia-verified.

entries.name: Gabonese popular music
entries.note: Gabonese popular music is an Afro-jazz and acoustic guitar-based genre developed in Libreville from the 1960s, drawing on Fang and Myene oral traditions alongside Congolese rumba influences; Pierre Akendengué established its international profile with French-language lyrics and acoustic arrangements, and younger artists have incorporated Afrobeat and urban contemporary styles.

research.period: Pierre Akendengué (b.1943) active from 1960s; MusicBrainz confirms Afrobeat tags.
research.geography: National scope; Libreville primary centre.
research.artists: Pierre Akendengué (b.1943, acoustic Afro-jazz), Annie-Flore Batchiellilys (b.1975), Lord Ekomy Ndong (b.1981, hip-hop). Wikipedia-verified.

entries.name: Togolese popular music
entries.note: Togolese popular music is a Lomé-centred genre that emerged in the 1970s, blending Ghanaian highlife, Congolese rumba, and local Ewe percussion traditions; Roger Damawuzan was the defining artist of the genre's formative decade, and contemporary Togolese musicians have integrated Afrobeats and urban gospel into an evolving popular scene.

research.period: MusicBrainz: Roger Damawuzan (b.1952) tagged highlife/Afrobeat; Togolese popular music. 1970s–present.
research.geography: National scope; Lomé primary centre.
research.artists: Roger Damawuzan (b.1952), Afia Mala, King Mensah (b.1974). Wikipedia-verified.

entries.name: Beninese popular music
entries.note: Beninese popular music is a Cotonou-centred genre that developed from the 1960s, drawing on Fon and Yoruba rhythmic traditions, Congolese guitar styles, and Cuban-influenced big-band arrangements; Gnonnas Pedro & His Dadjes Band were the genre's most internationally visible act, and contemporary Beninese artists participate in the pan-West African Afrobeats scene.

research.period: Gnonnas Pedro (1943-2004) active from 1960s; establishes genre date anchor.
research.geography: National scope; Cotonou and Porto-Novo primary centres.
research.artists: Gnonnas Pedro (1943-2004), Angélique Kidjo (b.1960), Sagbohan Danialou. Wikipedia-verified.

entries.name: Gambian popular music
entries.note: Gambian popular music is a Banjul-centred genre that combines the Mande kora-griot tradition with Western amplification and pop arrangements; Jaliba Kuyateh is the genre's most prominent practitioner, blending griot repertoire with dance rhythms for mass audiences, and the Gambia's small size has kept its popular scene closely tied to the broader Senegambian and West African pop market.

research.period: 1970s amplified kora-pop era. Ongoing.
research.geography: National scope; Banjul primary centre.
research.artists: Jaliba Kuyateh (b.1959), Foday Musa Suso (b.1953), Sona Jobarteh (b.1983). Wikipedia-verified.

entries.name: Sierra Leone afropop
entries.note: Sierra Leone afropop is a Freetown-centred popular genre that draws on the palm-wine guitar tradition of S.E. Rogie, Krio cultural identity, and West African highlife; post-civil-war reconstruction from 2002 brought a revived urban scene, and contemporary Sierra Leonean artists participate in the pan-African Afrobeats ecosystem while maintaining local Krio-language expression.

research.period: S.E. Rogie (1926-1994) from 1950s, but modern popular form consolidates 1970s.
research.geography: National scope; Freetown primary centre.
research.artists: S.E. Rogie (1926-1994), Emmerson Bockarie (b.1977), Jimmy B. Wikipedia-verified.

entries.name: Burkinabè popular music
entries.note: Burkinabè popular music is an Ouagadougou-centred genre that developed from the 1980s, combining Dyula and Mooré language traditions with Congolese soukous, Ghanaian highlife, and West African pop; rapper Smockey established the country's hip-hop scene in the 1990s, and the annual FESPACO film festival context has given Burkinabè artists regional visibility.

research.period: 1980s commercial pop era. Hip-hop from 1990s. Present.
research.geography: National scope; Ouagadougou primary centre.
research.artists: Smockey (b.1975), Victor Démé (b.1964, blues/pop), Floby (contemporary gospel-pop). Wikipedia-verified.

entries.name: Botswana popular music
entries.note: Botswana popular music is a Gaborone-centred genre influenced by neighbouring South African kwaito and house music, Setswana-language praise poetry, and kwasa kwasa dance rhythms from the DRC; the country's relatively high per-capita income has sustained a domestic recording industry, and Afro-pop acts participate in the regional Southern African popular scene.

research.period: 1990s urban pop scene. Kwaito influence from late 1990s. Present.
research.geography: National scope; Gaborone primary centre.
research.artists: Rre Joe Ngaka (veteran), Charma Gal (b.1989), Zeus (hip-hop). Wikipedia-partial.

entries.name: Malawian popular music
entries.note: Malawian popular music is a Blantyre and Lilongwe-centred genre that developed from the 1970s, blending Chichewa-language lyrics with Southern African guitar styles, Congolese soukous, and reggae influences; Lucius Banda established the genre's political dimension through protest music, and contemporary Malawian artists participate in the pan-African gospel and Afrobeats markets.

research.period: 1970s recorded popular music. Ongoing.
research.geography: National scope; Blantyre primary centre.
research.artists: Lucius Banda (b.1970), Billy Kaunda (b.1958), Evison Matafale (1970-2001). Wikipedia-verified.

entries.name: Mauritanian popular music
entries.note: Mauritanian popular music is rooted in the iggawen griot tradition of the Moorish Hassaniya-speaking community, in which hereditary musicians accompany the tidinit lute and ardin harp; Dimi Mint Abba brought this repertoire to international audiences from the 1970s, and contemporary artists such as Noura Mint Seymali integrate electronic production while maintaining Arabic-language maqam contours.

research.period: Dimi Mint Abba (1958-2011) debut late 1970s. Genre roots 1960s post-independence. Present.
research.geography: National scope; Nouakchott primary centre.
research.artists: Dimi Mint Abba (1958-2011), Noura Mint Seymali (b.1983), Malouma (b.1960). Wikipedia-verified.

entries.name: Libyan popular music
entries.note: Libyan popular music is a Tripoli-centred Arabic-language urban song genre that developed from the 1960s under radio broadcast sponsorship, blending Egyptian-influenced maqam melody with local Libyan rhythmic styles; Hamid Al-Shaeri relocated to Cairo and became a key architect of pan-Arab synthesiser pop in the 1980s, and Libyan artists continue to circulate in the North African and Gulf Arab music markets.

research.period: 1960s radio era. Hamid Al-Shaeri (b.1960) major figure from 1980s. Present.
research.geography: National scope; Tripoli primary centre.
research.artists: Hamid Al-Shaeri (b.1960), Mohamed Hasan, Ahmed Fakroun (b.1952). Wikipedia-verified.

entries.name: Somali popular music
entries.note: Somali popular music is a Mogadishu-centred genre that flourished from the 1960s through the 1980s in a 'golden age' of radio and theatre, blending Somali-language poetry with Egyptian, Cuban, and Indian film music influences; civil war from 1991 drove the scene into diaspora communities in Nairobi, London, and Minneapolis, where contemporary Somali hip-hop and R&B continue the tradition.

research.period: 1960s independence-era broadcasting. Golden age 1960s-1988. Diaspora continuation post-1991.
research.geography: National scope; diaspora scenes in Nairobi, London, Minneapolis.
research.artists: Hasan Adan Samatar (1941-2010), Magool (1948-2004), Waayaha Cusub (modern group). Wikipedia-verified.

entries.name: Sahrawi popular music
entries.note: Sahrawi popular music is a Hassaniya Arabic-language genre developed by communities of the Western Sahara diaspora, particularly in the Tindouf refugee camps in Algeria; it draws on tidinit lute and ardine harp traditions shared with Mauritania, and was brought to European audiences by Mariem Hassan in the 1980s–2000s, representing both cultural continuity and political expression for the Sahrawi people.

research.period: 1975 onset of displacement; diaspora scene. Mariem Hassan (1958-2015) key figure. Present.
research.geography: National scope (Western Sahara + Tindouf camps). Approximation to country scope.

entries.name: Comorian twarab
entries.note: Comorian twarab is an archipelago-specific variant of the East African tarabu tradition, performed at weddings and social celebrations in Shikomori and Arabic, combining oud accompaniment with call-and-response vocal textures; it developed its local character through French colonial and Arab seafaring contacts, and remains the dominant popular music form alongside ngoma percussion ceremonies.

research.period: Post-independence 1975 commercial scene; genre roots 1960s. Present.
research.geography: National scope; all four main islands.
research.artists: Abou Chihabi (veteran twarab), Nawal (b.1968, international crossover). Wikipedia-limited.

entries.name: Burundian popular music
entries.note: Burundian popular music is a Bujumbura-centred genre that developed from the 1970s alongside the famous royal drum (karyenda) tradition, blending Kirundi-language lyric forms with Congolese soukous guitar styles and East African rumba; post-2015 political instability has driven many artists into diaspora while a domestic scene continues through church-based gospel pop and youth-oriented urban music.

research.period: 1970s urban popular scene. Present (diaspora-sustained).
research.geography: National scope; Bujumbura primary centre.
research.artists: Khadja Nin (b.1962, Burundian-born internationally active), Ciza Muhire. Wikipedia-limited.

entries.name: Gumbé popular music
entries.note: Gumbé popular music is the urban popular form of Guinea-Bissau, taking its name and foundational percussion from the traditional gumbé frame drum; Super Mama Djombo pioneered the genre in the 1970s–1980s, combining independence-era revolutionary sentiment with Creole-language lyrics and electric guitar arrangements, and it remains the country's most distinctive popular export.

research.period: Super Mama Djombo active from mid-1970s; genre commercial form 1980s. Present.
research.geography: National scope; Bissau primary centre.
research.artists: Super Mama Djombo (formed 1974, peak 1980s), Dulce Maria Neves, Manecas Costa (b.1965). Wikipedia-verified.

entries.name: Solomon Islands string band
entries.note: Solomon Islands string band music is an acoustic popular genre that emerged in the 1960s from Melanesian adaptations of Hawaiian guitar and ukulele styles introduced by missionaries; performed in Pijin and regional languages, it combines guitar, ukulele, and bass guitar with harmonised vocals, and remains the most distinctively Solomon Islander popular form alongside imported reggae and hip-hop.

research.period: 1960s missionary/colonial contact era. Ongoing.
research.geography: National scope; Honiara primary centre.

entries.name: Contemporary famo
entries.note: Contemporary famo is the electrically amplified studio form of Lesotho's accordion-based popular genre, developed from the 1970s with electric bass and drum kit replacing traditional percussion; Puseletso Seema and later artists have released cassette and digital recordings for the Basotho diaspora market, maintaining famo's role as a vehicle for Sesotho cultural identity while modernising its production aesthetic.

research.period: 1970s electrified studio recording era. Ongoing.
research.geography: National scope; also diaspora in Johannesburg.

entries.name: Swazi popular music
entries.note: Swazi popular music is a Mbabane-centred genre that developed from the 1990s, drawing on South African kwaito and maskandi guitar styles and performed in siSwati; the small domestic market has meant Swazi artists typically circulate across the Southern African regional scene, and afrobeats influences have become prominent in the contemporary studio sound since the 2010s.

research.period: 1990s regional pop integration. Present.
research.geography: National scope; Mbabane primary centre.
research.artists: Bholoja (b.1975, siSwati soul), Vusi Nova (b.1984, SA-Swazi crossover). Wikipedia-limited.

entries.name: South Sudanese hip-hop
entries.note: South Sudanese hip-hop is a diaspora-rooted popular genre that developed in the mid-2000s, primarily in Nairobi and Western cities among South Sudanese refugees; Emmanuel Jal pioneered the form by addressing war, displacement, and reconciliation in English and Nuer, and following independence in 2011 a domestic Juba-based scene has emerged incorporating Dinka and Arabic influences.

research.period: Emmanuel Jal (b.1980) active from mid-2000s. Independence 2011 anchors domestic scene.
research.geography: National scope; Juba + diaspora (Nairobi, London, Canada).

entries.name: São Tomé puxa
entries.wikipedia_title: Music of São Tomé and Príncipe
entries.note: Puxa is the popular dance music of São Tomé and Príncipe, a Creole genre that blends African percussion, Portuguese colonial song, and Cuban and Brazilian influences; developed in São Tomé city from the 1970s post-independence era, it is performed for street celebrations alongside the older ússua and socopé rhythms, and remains the archipelago's most distinctively popular form.

research.period: 1975 independence; popular music from 1970s. Ongoing.
research.geography: National scope; São Tomé city primary centre.
research.artists: Gilberto Gil Umbelina, Armindo Neto. Wikipedia-limited.

entries.name: Cantopop
entries.note: Cantopop (Cantonese popular music) is the dominant popular genre of Macau, shared with Hong Kong, performed in Cantonese and marketed across the greater Guangdong and overseas Chinese diaspora; the genre consolidated in the mid-1970s through Hong Kong-produced cassettes and TV variety shows that circulated freely in Macau, and Portuguese colonial Macau developed its own small recording scene alongside the dominant Hong Kong mainstream.

research.period: 1974 marks the Cantopop boom (Sam Hui era). Macau participates via shared HK broadcast market.
research.geography: National scope; closely integrated with Hong Kong Cantopop market.
research.artists: Sandy Lam (b.1966, active Macau-HK), Faye Wong (b.1969), Leon Lai (b.1966). Mainstream HK-Macau Cantopop artists.
